newsitem.title: USA: Russian space probe plunge stirs some US jitters.
newsitem.headline: Russian space probe plunge stirs some US jitters.

text.p: The South Pacific swan-dive of a Russian Mars probe is causing some jitters in the U.S. space community, but some analysts feel occasional disasters like this are inevitable in the risky business of space.

"These things happen," said Michael Braukus, the chief NASA spokesman for an international space station project for which the Russians have contracted to provide the basic power supply. "It's a dangerous business."

Braukus discounted fears that Russia's unsettled political and economic climate could make for a rocky partnership in space, and noted that the United States also lost one of its Mars probes -- the Mars Observer -- shortly after launch earlier this year.
The $300 million Russian probe crashed into the Pacific Ocean off the Chilean coast on Monday, just over a day after launch, after failing to break free of Earth's orbit.
Russian officials said it was too early to determine the exact cause of the failure, and some wondered whether lack of funds had been a factor.

Money has been at the root of a spate of embarrassing problems for the Russian space programme, delaying supply missions to the orbiting Mir station, stranding U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid aboard it for weeks longer than expected and stalling salary payments to ground crews for months.

Because international cooperation is a source of funds for the cash-strapped Russians, the way they handle the investigation into the Mars probe mishap will be crucial, according to Mark Albrecht, a space business executive.

"The main question is, how open and candid are the Russians going to be?" said Albrecht, a vice president of the Virginia-based Science Applications International Corp., and formerly head of the White House National Space Council.
"If they are very reticent to discuss the accident, not very complete in their accounting, I think that could be a cause of great nervousness," Albrecht said.
The findings of any investigation will be important as well, he said in a telephone interview.

"If the cause turns out to be linked to "sloppy procedures or a distracted or dispirited workforce ... that would be a concern," Albrecht said. "If it turns out that this is one of those instances where there was a regrettable technical malfunction, it doesn't really matter."

Such technical problems are intrinsic to space exploration, said John Pike, head of the Space Policy Project at the private Federation of American Scientists. Ironically, he saw the flawed Mars-96 mission as a good sign for future ventures.
"The fact that the Russians were able to get this thing ready to go says they can get the job done even under adverse circumstances," Pike said in a telephone interview.

A long-time observer of U.S. and Russian space missions, Pike said the loss of an unstaffed launch vehicle -- especially one like the Russian Proton used on the Mars-96, which has previously been seen as highly reliable -- is no cause for global alarm.
"The bottom line is, on a good launch vehicle, you're going to lose one in 20, and this just happened to be it," Pike said.
But while such a failure may have been simply a function of the law of averages, Pike said it could have a salutary effect on space programme budgets in Russia.

"I hope that this is going to result in a little soul-searching in Moscow because they are going to have to come up with a little extra money to make sure their part of the space station is on time," Pike said.
The Russians are scheduled to launch the first element of the $17.4 billion international space station -- a custom-built power supply module -- in November 1997.
